fatal_errors: The proposed synchronized-reduction mechanism contradicts the supported sequential mechanism in which Pt, Ir, or Ru reduces first, establishes a lattice, and promotes reduction and incorporation of the remaining elements through dissociated hydrogen.
The intervention replaces the relevant spray-dried precursor and H2 reduction treatment with tailored organic ligands and an inert atmosphere.
The predicted universal FCC product misses Ru-directed HCP formation, Pt–Ru FCC/HCP coexistence, and thermally activated FCC-to-HCP conversion.
No supporting evidence or citations are supplied.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the general challenge of avoiding segregation in multielement alloys and proposes a genuinely testable ligand-control experiment. Its measurements could distinguish synchronized from asynchronous reduction, although the falsification rule should separately test kinetic synchronization and phase formation. Scientifically, however, it does not reconstruct the target system: the reported process operates in H2 near 300°C using compositionally uniform spray-dried salt particles, not ligand-matched precursors in an inert atmosphere at 150–250°C. Most importantly, formation is governed by intentionally asynchronous reduction: early Pt, Ir, or Ru nuclei provide both the parent lattice and surfaces that dissociate H2, allowing reactive hydrogen to reduce nearby base metals. Pd and noble-metal-free controls define the boundary. Crystal selection is also composition- and temperature-dependent, with Pt favoring FCC, Ru favoring HCP, and reheating enabling an FCC-to-HCP transition across an activation barrier. The generated answer predicts only FCC particles and omits these controls, phase-tuning boundaries, porous framework morphology, and catalytic outcomes. It is therefore a novel but unsupported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
